newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian refining margins seen weak for rest of 1990s. [CORRECTED 09:04 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Asian refining margins seen weak for rest of 1990s. [CORRECTED 09:04 GMT]

text.p: Refining margins in Asia are expected to remain narrow over the next five years which might make it difficult to justify new grassroots investments, analysts said on Monday.
They said the main factor pressuring margins will be petroleum products coming into Asia -- most noticeably from the Middle East.
The analysts were presenting papers at the Ninth Annual Refining Congress in Singapore on Monday.

"The key issue for Asia is no longer the difference between demand and refining capacity. The issue today is whether Asian demand will strain global supplies or not," Fereidun Fesharaki, director of the Hawaii-based East-West Center, told conference delegates.
"This will put tremendous pressure on merchant refineries, but will also delay new investments in refining everywhere," he said.
Refining margins fell steadily in Asia from the 1990/1991 Gulf War to a 10-year low in 1995.
Hydroskimming margins in 1995 were barely profitable, based on Arab Light crude refined in Singapore.

The East-West Center forecast these margins would rise to $1.00 per barrel in 1996 before falling over the next two years to around 50 cents per barrel. From 2000 until 2005, the Center forecast hydroskimming margins around $5.00 per barrel.

Cracking margins fell to under $3.50 per barrel in 1995 but could rise to $5.00 this year before falling again to just more than $4.00 in 1997 and 1998. Margins are seen around $7.00 for 2000 to 2005.
But this would not be sufficient for major investments in grassroot projects.
Asia's crude distillation capacity in 1995 was 16.02 million barrels per day (bpd). This could rise by (corrects from "to") 3.231 million bpd by 2000 based on planned refinery expansions.
But while product demand is strong, European and North American refineries will look to sell their products in Asia too.
"Globalization means that the Asian secret is out. As soon as you begin to make money, products will arrive from everywhere," Fesharaki said in his paper.

Jim Ayala, an analyst at consultancy McKinsey & Co, said product demand growth in Asia was strong at 4.1 percent per year by global standards, but the region's refining capacity was rising at a faster 4.6 to 5.1 per cent per year.
"Throughput will probably go up much faster, driven by China's plans to increase utilization," he said, through such measures as debottlenecking.
A big exporter to Asia will be the Middle East.
McKinsey & Co forecast Middle East products available for Asia would rise nine percent per year, or to 2.2 million bpd in the years to 2000 from 1.3 million in 1994.

Kuwait has been rebuilding its refining industry since the Gulf War, Abu Dhabi is increasingly export orientated and reform is likely to lead to lower product demand domestically in Saudi Arabia and Iran, the analysts said.
Other Middle East refiners are debottlenecking, upgrading or expanding.
But Ayala said investment in upgrading would keep pace with market needs as governments put in place legislation for lower sulphur and lighter products.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
